app.title: Atmospheric Light Laboratory
app.subtitle: Why the sky is blue, why sunsets are red, and why a well is dark

header.resetTitle: Return every control to its starting value

star.title: Light source (star)
star.temperatureHelp: Sets the emitted spectrum through Planck's law. Hotter stars emit relatively more short-wavelength light.
star.elevationHelp: How high the star stands. Lowering it lengthens the path light takes through the air.
star.realisticInsolationHelp: Scales the incoming light by how far this world orbits from its star, so planets can be compared honestly.
star.presetHelp: Chooses a star and sets its surface temperature. You can then fine-tune the temperature with the slider below.

atmosphere.title: Atmosphere
atmosphere.densityHelp: Multiplies the amount of all the air: gas, aerosol and ozone. 1 × is the world’s real value, 0 × is vacuum.
atmosphere.scaleHeightHelp: The height over which density falls by a factor of e. A larger H means a deeper, more gradual atmosphere.
atmosphere.aerosolHelp: Multiplies the amount of dust and droplets of the chosen kind. These particles scatter every colour almost equally and mostly forwards. 0 × means only the gas molecules scatter.
atmosphere.aerosolNative: As the chosen world has it
atmosphere.aerosolTypeHelp: Replaces the particles in the air with another kind (smog, desert dust, volcanic ash), keeping the same gas. The values follow aerosol types from the OPAC database.
atmosphere.exponentHelp: Scattering on molecules goes as 1/λⁿ. n = 4 is real air. At n = 0 the molecules scatter every colour equally and the sky loses its colour.
atmosphere.presetHelp: Chooses a planet or moon with its atmosphere. Resets density, aerosol and the exponent to that world’s values.

observer.title: Observer
observer.positionHelp: Above zero you climb through the atmosphere. Below zero you descend a shaft while the air above you stays exactly the same.
observer.viewDirectionHelp: Measured from straight up. 0 degrees is the zenith, 90 degrees is the horizon.
observer.wellDepthHelp: How deep the shaft is. The vertical position slider then goes down to the bottom at most.
observer.countShaftAirHelp: Off: the shaft is empty, and descending changes only how much sky you can see. On: the shaft fills with air whose gas grows denser with depth while its dust keeps the surface density; the light of the sky has to cross it.
observer.zoomHelp: How much of the world the cross-section shows. Zoom out at a low Sun to see the chord its light has to cross - that length is why it is red. The mouse wheel works too.
observer.wellEnabledHelp: Digs a vertical shaft the observer can descend. From the bottom you see only the part of the sky the walls do not hide.
observer.wellRadiusHelp: The radius of the shaft opening. Together with the observer’s depth it sets how wide a cone of sky is visible from the bottom: its half-angle is arctan(radius / depth).

rays.title: Rays and display
rays.showScatteringHelp: Off: the cross-section shows only the glow of the air and nothing is measured from rays; the values from theory remain.
rays.brightnessHelp: Multiplies how brightly the colours are shown, for example for dark Titan. It changes neither the calculation nor the hue.
rays.physicalMixHelp: Draw the families in the proportions the physics gives instead of the legible ones. Only about a sixth of the light crossing Earth’s air is scattered at all, so the picture fills with the unscattered beams that really do dominate it and the sky fan thins to almost nothing. Nothing measured changes — only what is drawn.
rays.countHelp: How many light paths are traced in the cross-section. The colour in the “What you see” box is measured from them: more rays give a more precise measurement but take longer.
rays.animateHelp: The rays are drawn progressively from the star to the observer. This changes nothing in the calculation.
rays.qualityHelp: How finely the theoretical values are computed (the table, the Theory tab, the glow of the air in the cross-section). The rays do not depend on it.

canvas.legendInCone: turns in view, but goes elsewhere
canvas.legendOffView: reaches you from elsewhere in the sky
canvas.rayLogEmpty: No ray selected. Click any ray in the cross-section.
canvas.skyStripHelp: The sky from horizon to horizon through the observer's own eyes. Black wedges are directions stopped by the shaft wall.

canvas.verticalExaggerated: Vertical scale is compressed so that both the shaft and the whole atmosphere fit on one picture.
canvas.legendStarlight: starlight from overhead, one ray each

spectrum.title: Spectrum
spectrum.empty: No light reaches the observer from this direction.

color.title: Perceived colour
color.computed: Computed from the spectrum through CIE 1931 XYZ, never chosen by hand.
color.blockedByWall: The shaft wall blocks this direction, so no light arrives at all.
color.darkness: Too little light to show a colour.
color.measured: What you see, measured from the rays
color.noneArrive: Not one ray comes down any of the {cast} directions in view.
color.noRays: No rays were traced in this direction.
color.measuredNote: Built only from the rays on screen, and it is the same calculation the strip under the picture uses - point the observer anywhere and the strip already shows this colour at that direction. The mix of the eight colours is the hue; how many of them there are, against how much sky the field of view still holds, is the brightness. Climbing leaves fewer rays because there is less air overhead to scatter; a shaft leaves less sky because the rock takes the directions. Too little light reads as dark. Brown means something else entirely: that you are facing the rock.
color.agreement: The integrator differs by dxy = {dxy}; brightness ratio {ratio} from {rays} rays.
color.belowOneRay: Less light than one ray stands for, across {cast} directions in view.
color.starInCone: The star is in your field of view: its disc is about {ratio} times brighter than the sky around it, so the bundle on the picture is not to scale and cannot be.
color.overheadStarShaft: The shaft has hidden {lost} of your view of the sky, but the patch of sky behind the star is as bright as up top, so it has changed nothing in this ratio.
color.overheadStarOut: A star straight overhead, as bright as Vega, is outside your field of view. Look straight up.
color.overheadStarPercent: A star straight overhead, as bright as Vega, has only {pct} of the brightness of the patch of sky around it (1′ across, the smallest detail the eye resolves).
color.overheadStarTimes: A star straight overhead, as bright as Vega, is {n} times brighter than the patch of sky around it (1′ across, the smallest detail the eye resolves).
color.overheadStarBlack: A star straight overhead, as bright as Vega: the patch of sky around it is black.
color.starVisible: Neither the sky behind it nor the lit surroundings outshine it, so it can be seen.
color.starBorderline: It is at the edge of visibility: only an experienced observer who knows where to look will find it.
color.starLost: The sky behind it is far brighter, so the star is lost in it.
color.starGlare: The sky behind it will not hide it, but the sunlit ground around you is brighter: an eye adjusted to it and to the Sun will not catch the star. From a shadow, where you see neither the sunlit ground nor the Sun, it would be visible.

data.title: Physical quantities
data.advancedOnly: Switch to Advanced level to see the full readout.

daySky.see: The sky glows blue in every direction away from the star, while the star itself still looks close to white. Nothing here is painted blue: you are looking at sunlight that has been knocked sideways out of the beam by air molecules.
daySky.why: Air molecules scatter light more strongly the shorter its wavelength, roughly as 1/λ⁴: about {ratio} times more strongly at 450 nm than at 650 nm. So the light reaching your eye from the sky is mostly blue. The direct beam keeps almost all of its red, which is why the Sun looks warm white.

greySky.see: The sky is greyish white, not blue, although roughly as much light comes from it.
greySky.why: The exponent n is {exponent}, so the molecules scatter every wavelength almost equally: the ratio of scattering at 450 nm to that at 650 nm is only {ratio}. The scattered light then has the same mix of colours as sunlight, so it is white. What makes the sky blue is only that short wavelengths are scattered more strongly.

sunset.see: The star has dropped low, turned orange to red, and dimmed sharply. The colour change is not in the star but in the path its light takes through the air: {airmass} times longer than straight up.
sunset.why: The share of light that gets through the air is T = e^(−τ), where the optical depth τ grows with the amount of air on the way. Along this path τ = {tau450} at 450 nm but only {tau650} at 650 nm, so blue is filtered out almost completely while red gets through. What you see is the leftover of the beam, not new red light.

greySunset.see: The star has dropped low and dimmed sharply, but it has not turned red. Its light crosses {airmass} times more air than straight up, but the air now takes away every colour almost equally.
greySunset.why: Along the path τ at 450 nm ({tau450}) is almost the same as at 650 nm ({tau650}), so by T = exp(−τ) roughly the same share of each colour gets through. A long path alone does not colour a sunset; that needs air that weakens blue more than red.

twilight.see: The star is below the horizon. Direct light no longer reaches you, yet the sky is not black: it is lit only by air high above you that is still in sunlight.
twilight.why: The shadow of the planet has swallowed the lower atmosphere, so the scattering integral collects light only from the illuminated layers higher up. That light has crossed the ozone layer edgeways, and ozone absorbs orange and yellow (the Chappuis band): this, more than Rayleigh scattering alone, is what keeps the twilight zenith blue (Hulburt 1953). Real twilight is also brighter than a single scattering can make it, because light is scattered several times on the way, and the purple glow of some evenings is red sunlight scattered forward by haze in the stratosphere.

highAltitude.see: The sky above you has gone much darker and deeper in colour. The star has not changed and you have not left the atmosphere, but far less air remains overhead.
highAltitude.why: The column above you falls exponentially, C(z) = C(0) exp(−z/H). At {z} with H = {scaleHeight} only {columnPercent} of the air is left above you, so there is proportionally less material to scatter light towards your eye.

space.see: The sky is completely black although the star shines as brightly as before and has a sharp edge against the dark. Plenty of light is passing you; there is simply nothing here to scatter it towards your eye.
space.why: The scattering integral has collapsed to zero because ρ → 0. Brightness of the sky needs a medium, not a source. This is why astronauts in daylight see a black sky, and why the same is true on the airless Moon.

airless.see: It is full daylight, the ground is brightly lit, and yet the sky directly overhead is black. Nothing is blocking the light - there is simply no air to scatter it.
airless.why: With ρ = 0 every term in the scattering integral vanishes, while the direct transmission stays T = 1. A black sky proves the absence of a scattering medium, never the absence of light.

thinAir.see: The sky is almost black with a hint of deep blue, and yet it is daytime and the ground is brightly lit. There is air here, but it is very thin.
thinAir.why: Rayleigh scattering works just as it does on Earth and still favours blue by 1/λ⁴. But the optical depth is only {tau550}, so only a few thousandths of the passing light are scattered. The colour stays blue; only the brightness goes.

wellShallow.see: You have dropped into the shaft. The patch of sky through the mouth is exactly as bright and exactly as blue as it was outside - but it is now a small disc instead of the whole sky, and everything around you has darkened.
wellShallow.why: The air above you has not changed at all: C_atm is still C_atm(0). What changed is geometry. A ray leaving at zenith angle θ escapes only while tan(θ) ≤ R/d. Here that limit is {aperture}, leaving {solidAngle} of sky out of a full hemisphere.

wellDeep.see: Deep in the shaft it is nearly dark, yet the scrap of sky far above is as blue as it is at the surface. The darkness is not caused by the air but by seeing the sky only through a small opening.
wellDeep.why: Radiance in the open direction is unchanged, but the illuminance follows the visible solid angle: E/E_open = sin²(θ_max) = {ratio}. Compare this with climbing: at {z} up, the sky itself would be dimmer because the air column really did shrink.

dusty.see: The sky is pale ochre rather than blue, and the light is soft and diffuse. Larger particles are doing the scattering here, and they treat every colour almost alike.
dusty.why: Aerosols scatter with only a weak wavelength dependence (roughly 1/λ⁰ to 1/λ¹) and a strongly forward-peaked Henyey-Greenstein lobe with g = {g}. Where the dust also absorbs blue more than red, as on Mars, the sky turns warm.

denseAtmosphere.see: The light down here is dim and heavily tinted. Very little of the original spectrum survives the journey to the surface.
denseAtmosphere.why: The optical depth is far above one, so exp(−τ) has extinguished the short wavelengths entirely. Note that a single-scattering model under-predicts the true brightness here: in reality photons scatter many times before arriving.

coldStar.see: The star is orange and the sky above it is beige to a dull grey-blue. It is bluer than the star, but not as blue as under the Sun.
coldStar.why: Rayleigh scattering still prefers short wavelengths by 1/λ⁴, but the star emits little short-wavelength light for it to work on. The sky colour is the product of the scattering law and the source spectrum, not the scattering law alone.

hotStar.see: The star is blue-white and the sky is an intense deep blue, noticeably stronger than under a Sun-like star.
hotStar.why: A hot black body emits far more short-wavelength light, and the 1/λ⁴ law then amplifies that excess. Source spectrum and scattering law multiply together.

compare.controlsHelp: Which simulation the left-hand panel drives. The other stays exactly as it is. Clicking a panel selects it too.
compare.enableHelp: Adds a second simulation, entire: its own star, its own atmosphere, its own observer, its own rays and its own strip of sky beneath the picture.
compare.note: {observer} — the star, the air and the observer below are its own, and so are the numbers on the right.
compare.selected: selected - the controls drive this one
compare.sharedRays: This section drives both simulations. It sets how they are drawn rather than what is computed; two panels at two exposures could not be compared by eye.
compare.syncAtoBHelp: Copies the whole of A onto B: star, atmosphere and observer. Both panels then stand on the same footing, so you can change exactly one thing.
compare.syncBtoAHelp: Copies the whole of B onto A: star, atmosphere and observer.
compare.title: Two simulations

footer.modelNote: Light is followed from the star to one scattering event and then to the eye. Multiple scattering and refraction are not modelled.

histogram.title: Light the drawn rays deliver
histogram.help: The spectrum measured from the rays above, not computed from theory. Filled bars: light arriving at the observer, coloured from the viewing cone and grey from the rest of the sky. Dashed outline: the unscattered direct beam, scaled to its own peak because it is thousands of times brighter. The scale is held at the brightest sky seen so far, so climbing makes the bars fall.

panel.pathInfo: Path through the air {km} km, air mass {airmass}.
panel.budgetTitle: Where the light of each colour went
panel.budgetTooltip: got through {t}, scattered by molecules {r}, scattered by aerosol {a}, absorbed by ozone {o}, absorbed by aerosol {x}
panel.budgetNote: Each row is one colour; 100 % is the light of that colour above the atmosphere. Scattered light does not vanish: it leaves sideways and glows as the sky.
panel.chamberNote: With few rays the counted share differs from the calculation by chance. The calculation is e^(−τ) for the beam’s whole path.
panel.refractionText: Refraction lifts the Sun by {arcmin}′. Its blue image sits {arcsec}″ above its red one, because the refractive index of air is about 1.5 % larger for blue. For comparison: the Sun is about 32′ across.
panel.principlesTitle: What the air does to light

molecules.text: The light's electric field sets the electrons in an air molecule oscillating, and the molecule sends out light of the same colour in new directions. The light is not lost; it changes direction. Molecules (about 0.3 nm) are far smaller than the wavelength of light (400–700 nm), and for such small particles scattering grows as 1/λ⁴: blue (450 nm) is scattered about 4.5 times as strongly as red (650 nm).

haze.text: Droplets and dust grains are about as large as the wavelength or larger. They scatter mostly forwards and treat the colours much more evenly than molecules do (blue at most about twice as strongly as red), which is why haze looks whitish. Cloud droplets are larger still and scatter every colour alike: clouds are white.

absorption.text: Ozone and soot take light out of the beam and turn it into heat. Ozone absorbs mainly yellow and orange. In clean air this is a small part of what the beam loses.

path.text: The same amount of air always removes the same share of the light that enters it, so the light that gets through falls exponentially with the air crossed: I = I₀·e^(−τ). The lower the Sun, the more air; blue goes first, so the Sun turns yellow, orange and red. The blue taken out of the beam has not vanished: seen from the side, it is the blue sky.

refraction.text: Air also bends light, blue about 1.5 % more than red. Near the horizon this lifts the Sun by about half a degree and gives it coloured rims and the green flash. It does not make the setting Sun red: scattering does.

views.text: Beam through the air shows how much of each colour is lost, and where. Collisions up close shows how it happens to single rays: a ray that meets nothing stays in the Sun’s beam, a scattered one becomes light of the sky, an absorbed one is gone.

chosen.title: The chosen ray

does.rayleigh: The light sets the molecule's electrons oscillating, and the molecule sends it out again in a new direction; here the ray is turned by {deg}°. No light is lost, but it no longer travels towards the observer. Molecules do this to blue light several times as often as to red (1/λ⁴); seen from the side, this light is the blue sky.
does.aerosolScatter: The grain scatters the light too, but mostly forwards; here the ray is turned by {deg}°. Grains are much larger than molecules and treat the colours much more evenly, so haze whitens the sky and makes a bright glow round the Sun.
does.aerosolAbsorb: The grain absorbs the light: its energy warms the grain and the air around it, and the ray ends here. Dark grains absorb every colour, blue a little more.
does.ozone: Ozone absorbs the light, most strongly yellow and orange (the Chappuis band): its energy warms the air and the ray ends here. Ozone hardly absorbs blue light.

again.rayleigh: Another molecule scatters it again; here the ray is turned by {deg}°.
again.aerosolScatter: Another grain scatters it again; here the ray is turned by {deg}°.

end.direct: It met nothing and reached the detector in its original direction. It is part of the direct sunlight: the light of the Sun's disc itself.
end.absorbed: Its energy stayed in the air; the light is gone.

scattered.detector: It reached the far wall, but from a different direction than the Sun's. It no longer belongs to the Sun's disc: an observer sees it as light from the sky.
scattered.top: It left the beam sideways, through the top of the chamber. Light scattered like this is what an observer looking at this piece of air from the side sees: the sky.
scattered.bottom: It left the beam sideways, through the bottom of the chamber. Light scattered like this is what an observer looking at this piece of air from the side sees: the sky.
scattered.back: It was turned back towards the Sun. Part of the light scattered back like this leaves the Earth again; it is one reason the Earth looks blue from space.
scattered.inside: We stop following it after {n} collisions; it no longer belongs to the direct beam.

chosen.compare: Switching colour keeps the same ray, entering at the same height: it passes the same particles, but their targets are a different size for it. Blue rays hit something far more often than red ones.
chosen.target: For {nm} nm a molecule’s target is {ratio}× as wide as for red ({red} nm), because molecules scatter this colour {ratio}× as strongly.
